text: Campaign started. v6e quota is 512 on-demand and 1536 spot, but a nine-zone sweep found multi-chip capacity in only two zones: us-east1-d and asia-northeast1-b.
detail: us-east5-a/b/c, us-south1-a and us-central1-a all refuse v6e-4 and v6e-8 with 'no more capacity'. Single chips are available almost everywhere. Quota is not capacity.

text: A TensorCore row gather of 1M indices from a 4.2M-row table runs at 1.3 GB/s, which is 0.08% of the chip's 1,600 GB/s of HBM bandwidth.
detail: This is the headroom the whole study is about. Gemini's read: HBM transaction granularity means a random small-row read pulls a wide line and discards most of it, predicting sorted or block-contiguous indices could recover roughly 10x. Untested.

text: The first fabric numbers were my own harness, not the fabric. A 0.55 ms floor appeared identically for two different collectives at four payload sizes, which is the signature of host dispatch.
detail: Fixed by chaining 32 collectives inside one jit and dividing. Corrected all_to_all at 0.25 MiB: 0.027 ms of fabric under 0.53 ms of dispatch. The uncorrected figure was 20x too high.

text: Host dispatch costs 0.51 ms at 0.25 MiB rising to 1.23 ms at 16 MiB, up to 20x the cost of the collective itself.
detail: Scale-independent and actionable: small collectives on TPU are orchestration-bound rather than network-bound. This is what an on-chip collectives engine like TPU 8i's CAE exists to remove.

text: all_to_all at 16 MiB per chip is free from 8 to 16 chips (+1%) and then costs +77% at 32 chips: 0.236, 0.239, 0.423 ms.
detail: Measured on a v6e-32 in us-east1-d, median of 20 samples, dispatch amortised.

text: My host-boundary explanation for the +77% is probably wrong. Gemini proposes bisection congestion, which fits better.
detail: 16 chips is likely a 4x4 torus and 32 a 4x8. The bisection cut stays 4 links wide while injected data doubles, so the same physical bottleneck carries twice the traffic. Test: run a 16-chip sub-communicator on the 32-chip slice at identical payload. If it stays fast, the effect is scaling and congestion rather than slice shape.

text: A collective costs 1.37x to 1.62x more while the MXU is busy: 1.62x at 8 chips, 1.61x at 16, 1.37x at 32.
detail: This is the number that matters to anyone running thousands of chips, because step-time models are built from idle microbenchmarks. Tail was tight, p99/p50 = 1.00, on a single-tenant slice.

text: Burst a v6e-256 once for the scaling curve instead of running a larger steady fleet, and delete it from a shell trap.
detail: A 256-chip slice costs about $359/hour on spot. A third point on the curve is the most valuable data available to us, and leaving the slice running is the most expensive mistake available, so the delete is unconditional.

text: Reframed from 'benchmark SparseCore' to 'where does irregular work belong, in a local gather engine or on the wire'.
detail: Gemini's objection: TPU 8i deletes four SparseCores and adds a collectives engine, so SparseCore looks like a deprecating branch. Half right. 8t keeps SparseCore and v7x has it, so the unit is being split by role: training keeps local gather, inference moves it to the fabric. That makes the boundary itself the research question.

text: Methodology, recorded deliberately. This campaign is run by Claude Code on Opus 5 with a 1M context, using background tasks for concurrent TPU jobs, launchd for a 20-minute measurement cycle, and Gemini 3.1 Pro as an adversarial advisor on framing and confounds.
detail: Gemini has changed the direction twice: it identified SparseCore as a possibly deprecating branch, and it replaced my host-boundary explanation with bisection congestion. Both are logged as corrections. This is the same shape as Discovery Loop, the public benefit corporation Jeff Dean, Sanjay Ghemawat, Oriol Vinyals and Quoc Le launched on 5 August 2026 to automate the propose-run-evaluate loop, with hardware design named as a target domain. The notable part is that the loop is now cheap enough for one student to run.

text: all_to_all per-op cost is flat from 16 to 256 chips at fixed per-chip payload: 0.421, 0.424, 0.431, 0.438, 0.438 ms for 16, 32, 64, 128, 256 chips at 16 MiB.
detail: Measured on a v6e-256 in us-east1-d, 64 hosts, during a 2.6-minute burst before the slice was deleted. Bandwidth-bound all-to-all does not care how many participants there are once past the local neighbourhood.

text: The +77% inflection I attributed to a host boundary was wrong, and the 256-chip run proves it. The same 16 chips cost 0.239 ms when carved from a 32-chip slice and 0.421 ms when carved from a 256-chip slice.
detail: Same payload, same participant count, 1.76x apart. So the cost is set by the physical geometry the sub-communicator sits in, not by N. This is the sub-communicator control experiment Gemini proposed, performed accidentally by running the same sweep on two slice sizes. Gemini's bisection-congestion explanation survives; mine does not.

text: Carving a sub-communicator out of a slice is penalised, and using the whole slice is not. all_reduce at 0.25 MiB costs 0.208 ms on 128 of 256 chips but only 0.056 ms on all 256.
detail: 3.7x, in favour of the full slice. Likely XLA selecting a different collective algorithm when the participant set matches the native topology. Directly actionable for anyone partitioning a pod between jobs: a job whose chips do not form a natural sub-torus pays for it in every collective.

text: Small all_reduce degrades with participants while all_to_all does not. At 0.25 MiB, all_reduce goes 0.066, 0.113, 0.208 ms across 32, 64, 128 chips, while all_to_all goes 0.037, 0.040, 0.047.
detail: Latency-bound reductions grow with chip count; bandwidth-bound exchanges stay flat. The two primitives have opposite scaling characters, which is a clean argument for why training and inference silicon diverged.

text: all_reduce failed with an XLA INTERNAL RET_CHECK error on 8-chip and 16-chip sub-communicators of the 256-chip slice, 8 of 48 configurations.
detail: all_to_all succeeded on the same meshes, and the same all_reduce configurations worked on the 32-chip slice. Worth a minimal reproduction and possibly a JAX or XLA issue.

text: Target the Anthropic TPU Kernel Engineer and Performance Engineer, Inference Systems roles with this work.
detail: Their posted scope is almost a description of this study: accelerator kernels, collective communication, kernel overheads, tail latency, and tracing a regression from request timing through routing and batching down into kernel overhead. This campaign measures dispatch overhead, collective cost, MXU interference and tail latency on the exact hardware Anthropic runs on, given the 3.5 GW of Google compute coming online for them in 2027.

text: Negative result, and a decisive one: the Pallas SparseCore gather does not compile on v6e. Seven shape and dtype variants all fail with 'tpu.enqueue_indirect_dma op Not implemented', 'sc_tpu.enqueue_transfer op Not implemented', or a CompileTimeSparseCore alloca error.
detail: The API imports and get_sparse_core_info() reports 2 cores, 16 subcores, 8 lanes on v6e, so the hardware is there and the Python surface is there, but the Mosaic lowering for indirect DMA is not implemented for this generation in JAX 0.10.2. The JAX documentation uses a TPU 7x system for its examples. Conclusion: SparseCore kernel work needs Ironwood, which we do not have. This closes the local-gather half of the study on our hardware.

text: Question chosen: does the SHAPE of an allocation matter more than its SIZE? The SparseCore path is unavailable, and the topology result is the strongest thing we have.
detail: Three measurements already support it: identical 16 chips cost 1.76x differently depending on whether they were carved from a 32-chip or a 256-chip slice; a 128-chip sub-communicator costs 3.7x more than using all 256; and all_to_all is otherwise flat from 16 to 256 chips. This is directly actionable for anyone partitioning a pod between jobs, it is checkable against TPU 8i's claim that a high-radix 7-hop fabric reduces exactly this sensitivity, and it does not depend on any unimplemented API.

text: Billing balance is not readable by this account. qanh@stanford.edu has no permission on billing account 01F867-B7EAEB-2BA7E1, and there is no BigQuery billing export visible.
detail: So spend tracking is budget_guard.py's estimate: live chips times wall time times the spot rate, deliberately over-billing when a slice is preempted mid-interval. The real balance has to come from whoever owns the class billing account.

text: Verification failed on three fronts and most of today's latency numbers are not yet trustworthy. Recording this before any of them reach a writeup.
detail: 1) Timing method not converged: per-op cost varies 2.11x with how many ops are chained (0.1418 ms at INNER=8, 0.0774 at 32, 0.0672 at 64), so quoted ms/op figures are overestimates and cross-config comparisons are only valid if residual overhead is constant, which is unproven. 2) Sub-mesh collectives on a multi-process slice may be invalid: a 'reversed' 8-chip subset measured 0.0042 ms for a 16 MiB all_to_all, which would be about 3.5 TB/s per chip and is not physical. 3) The gather harness is non-monotonic: dim=32 random reads 4.97 GB/s while dim=8 reads 8.79, and sequential access measures slower than random, which cannot be right.

text: The geometry result is contaminated, and the topology dump proves it. 'contiguous' and 'reversed' are both compact 4x2 blocks with identical Manhattan diameter 4, yet measured 0.2368 and 0.0042 ms, 56x apart.
detail: Identical geometry cannot produce a 56x difference, so the fast number is an artifact of the sub-mesh, not a placement effect. What survives as plausible: strided and shuffled subsets have diameter 8 against contiguous diameter 4 and measured slower (0.416 and 0.419 against 0.239 ms at n=16). That is consistent with a real diameter effect but cannot be claimed until sub-meshes are validated. The earlier 1.76x and 3.7x sub-communicator results used the same construction and inherit the same doubt.

text: Falsified: sorting the indices does not recover TPU gather bandwidth. Gemini predicted roughly 10x; measured is 1.00x.
detail: At dim=1 and dim=8, random, sorted, blocked and sequential index orders are within 1% of each other. So the 1.3 GB/s figure is not about index locality, and the HBM-transaction-waste explanation does not survive in this form. The dim=32 rows are excluded because that part of the harness is inconsistent.

text: Freeze new data collection on latency until the method is validated. Three fixes first: converge the amortisation by sweeping INNER to a plateau, validate sub-meshes with process_allgather correctness checks before trusting any sub-communicator number, and rebuild the gather harness so absolute bandwidth is monotonic in row width.
detail: Collecting more numbers with a harness that fails its own checks just produces a larger pile of wrong numbers. The campaign keeps running because repeated sweeps on fresh slices are still useful as a variance and capacity dataset, which does not depend on the absolute latency being right.

text: There is no TPU secondary market and the barrier is contractual, not technical. GPU capacity trades on Vast.ai, RunPod, SF Compute and Prime Intellect at 50 to 70% below hyperscaler rates; TPU capacity trades nowhere.
detail: Three compounding reasons: nobody outside Google owns TPU hardware to list, the GCP terms forbid resale in plain language, and the favourable price per FLOP exists to capture the workload, which a secondary market would leak. Our $1.4033 per v6e chip-hour is roughly 2x an A100 80GB and 0.7x an H100 SXM on marketplace rates, while v6e is 918 BF16 TFLOPS against A100's 312. That gap would normally be arbitraged away and cannot be.

text: Google's answer to the missing market is to move the primary one: direct TPU hardware sales to selected customers from 2027, a sanctioned Blackstone TPU cloud announced May 2026, and 8t/8i shipping with TorchTPU, vLLM, SGLang and bare-metal access.
detail: Unbundling the chip from the cloud on Google's own schedule and terms, which is what a resale market would have done without either. Alphabet has cited 2027 for third-party hardware sales and an ambition of up to 10% of NVIDIA datacenter revenue.

text: No capacity will be listed or sold from this billing account. The market question is answered as analysis instead, which is the publishable part.
detail: The account belongs to the class, the terms prohibit resale explicitly, and losing the account ends the study. The analysis needed no transaction: the absence of the market is itself the result, and it explains why TPU pricing can sit structurally below GPU market rates.

text: We hold 33 of the 41 TPU chips in the entire class project. One peer holds 8, in us-west4-a. Nobody holds anything in us-east5.
detail: So the 'no more capacity' refusals in us-east5-a, -b and -c are Google's limit at our tier, not contention with classmates. That attribution is only possible because soe-hpccenter is a shared project where every member can list every TPU, which makes it a natural experiment in capacity contention: roughly fifty students, one quota grant, observable continuously. Peer names are hashed in the published series.

text: Our tier is Spot, confirmed from the machines: schedulingConfig.spot is True on both slices, no reservation, no queued resource, and we lack permission to list reservations.
detail: Lowest priority, no SLA, preemptible at any moment, which is why the first probe died inside 27 minutes. We do hold 512 chips of on-demand quota at $2.70/chip-hr, 1.92x the spot price, if a run ever needs stability more than volume. For a measurement campaign, spot is correct: preemption costs cycles but variance across freshly-placed slices is itself data.

text: Banked 615.6 MiB of HLO modules and profiler traces for 12 configurations, then pulled them off the spot slice to the laptop as a 118 MB archive.
detail: Access to this hardware ends with the course credit. Summary numbers cannot answer 'was that XLA's algorithm choice or a hardware limit' after the fact; a compiled HLO module can. Perishable data first, analysis later, because the analysis does not need the chips and the capture does.

text: Supervisor now also records project-wide contention, rebuilds the logbook and pushes every cycle, so the public page updates itself without anyone editing it.
detail: Cycle order is: bill the budget, reclaim capacity if preempted, measure, observe the shared project, regenerate, publish.

text: Paying more does not conjure chips. An on-demand v6e-8 in us-east5-a was refused with the same capacity error as spot, so both tiers draw the same physical pool.
detail: Widely assumed otherwise: on-demand is often treated as jumping the queue. At 1.92x the price ($2.70 against $1.4033 per chip-hour) it bought nothing in an exhausted zone. Exhaustion is physical, not priority-based, at least for v6e in us-east5 in August 2026.

text: The only other TPU in the class project is a single v5litepod-8 held by one peer in us-west4-a since 14 August. Nobody else holds v6e anywhere.
detail: So capacity contention within the class is not the constraint on this study, and the two facts together are informative: the v6e shortage is Google-side, while the one peer sits on the previous generation in the zone the course labs used. Peer identity stays out of the published series; project members can see it themselves.

text: Generalised the burst pattern into burst.sh, which claims a parent slice of a given size, runs the sweep plus the geometry run plus artifact capture, then deletes from a trap.
detail: The geometry question needs the same subset size measured from several different parents, since 16 chips carved from a 32 and from a 256 already differ by 1.76x. One parent per burst, and the delete is unconditional because a forgotten large slice is the most expensive possible mistake.

text: The impossible 0.0042 ms is explained: the 'reversed' layout selects the LAST devices, which belong to the highest-numbered processes, so process 0 owns none of them and times a no-op while the other processes do the work.
detail: Confirmed by the 64-chip parent, where 'shuffled' also produced 0.0042 ms for n=8 because that permutation likewise excluded process 0's devices. The methodological rule for multi-host JAX benchmarking: the process doing the timing must own devices in the mesh. Any subset measurement that violates it is meaningless, and this study produced several before catching it.

text: With that artifact excluded, the geometry effect is real and reproduced on a third parent size. Sixteen chips at identical payload cost 0.2390 ms carved from a 32-chip slice and 0.4217 ms carved from a 64-chip slice, while the strided layout inverts: 0.4160 against 0.2260.
detail: So up to 1.9x at fixed participant count and fixed bytes, decided by how the subset sits inside its parent, and the ordering between layouts flips with parent size. That is the study's central claim and it now has three parent sizes behind it (32, 64, 256). It also means a scheduler handing out 16 chips can hand out something 1.9x slower without either party knowing.

text: Non-preemptible capacity is not available to us at all. An on-demand v6e-1 in us-east1-d fails with 'User does not have permission to submit requests for accelerator type v6e-1 in location us-east1-d', while the same request in us-east5-a fails with genuine capacity exhaustion.
detail: Two different refusals that were briefly conflated. In us-east5 both tiers hit an empty pool, so paying more buys nothing there. In us-east1-d, the zone that does have capacity, the project simply lacks on-demand permission for v6e. Conclusion: there is no path to avoiding preemption on this account, which is why every experiment is built to survive it.

text: Dropped to low-burn: the steady fleet is one v6e-1 at $1.40/hr, with multi-chip work happening only in explicit bursts that delete themselves. Runway is now past Sept 1 by a wide margin.
detail: At 97 chips the runway was five days. Spent so far is about $58 of $17,000. Multi-chip slices are claimed for a specific queued experiment and released the moment it finishes, which is both cheaper and better science than an idle fleet.

text: Added an hourly availability probe across eight zones, recording whether a v6e-8 can be claimed and deleting immediately when it can.
detail: Every capacity claim in this study was measured around 04:00 on a Sunday, which is when enterprise demand is lowest. Two weeks of hourly probes turns that caveat into a dataset: when can a student on a shared project actually get TPU capacity, by hour and by weekday. Failed probes are free and successful ones live about ninety seconds.

text: The central result now has a mechanism, confirmed against Google's published v6e topology. v6e-16 is 4x4, v6e-32 is 4x8, v6e-64 is 8x8, v6e-256 is 16x16, all 2D torus.
detail: Bisection width in a 2D torus is 2 x min(X,Y) links: 8 for 4x4, 8 for 4x8, 16 for 8x8, 32 for 16x16. So going 16 to 32 chips doubles the injected traffic while the bisection cut stays 8 links wide, and our measured all_to_all jumps 1.77x (0.239 to 0.423 ms). From 32 chips onward bisection doubles as chips double, and the measurement goes flat: 0.423, 0.431, 0.438 ms for 32, 64, 256 chips, +4% across an eightfold increase. The mechanism predicted the flatness before the 256-chip burst measured it.

text: Gemini's bisection hypothesis was right in detail, including the specific topologies it guessed. It said '16 chips is likely a 4x4 torus and 32 a 4x8' from first principles; Google's documentation says exactly that.
detail: My host-boundary explanation is now fully retired. Worth recording that the adversarial reviewer out-predicted the person holding the hardware, and that the confirmation came from a specification sheet rather than from more measurement.

text: Our absolute numbers verify against published specs. v6e is documented at 1,638 GB/s of HBM and 800 GB/s of ICI per chip.
detail: The TensorCore row gather reached 1.3 GB/s, which is 0.079% of documented HBM bandwidth, so the headline 0.08% figure is exact rather than rhetorical. Peak measured all_reduce bus bandwidth was 158 GB/s at 256 chips, a defensible fraction of a ring's usable share of 800 GB/s at 16 MiB messages, which is well short of the asymptotic regime. Nothing in our data exceeds a documented limit, which is the minimum bar for believing a harness.

text: The token market has already competed below our cost basis, so selling inference was never economic regardless of the terms. DeepSeek V4 Flash, the current OpenRouter usage leader, sells output at $0.123 per million tokens with a 1M context.
detail: Matching that at $1.4033 per chip-hour requires 3,175 tokens per second per chip. Against the earlier $0.95/M reference the break-even was 410 tokens/s/chip, so the leader is roughly 8x below what a student on spot pricing could achieve. Pulled live from the OpenRouter models API, which lists 413 models; 57 are in the open-weight families.

text: Next experiment is dense against MoE on identical chips: Qwen3.8-27B at 27B dense versus Qwen3-30B-A3B at 30B total and 3B active. Near-identical total parameters, opposite communication profiles.
detail: This is the study's thesis applied to a real workload rather than a microbenchmark. The MoE model pays an all-to-all tax on every token that the dense model does not, and we now have the fabric cost curve and its bisection mechanism to predict what that tax should be. Serving throughput is secondary; the comparison is the point, which is why it does not matter that we cannot beat market token prices.

text: Google's TPU serving stack is not installable from PyPI as published. tpu-inference 0.26.0 pins libtpu==0.0.43, a version that was never published: PyPI jumps from 0.0.42.1 to 0.0.45.
detail: Reproduced on a v6e host with python 3.11. Version 0.25.0 installs cleanly, so only the current release is broken. This is a one-line fix on Google's side and a hard wall for anyone trying to serve on TPU today, which is worth a bug report.

text: The vLLM wheel on PyPI is a CUDA build that cannot import on a TPU host, and it pins torch==2.13 while tpu-inference pins torchax and jax 0.10.2 with no PyTorch at all. Installing both loosely downgrades torch and breaks vLLM.
detail: So the real TPU serving stack is jax 0.10.2, jaxlib 0.10.2, libtpu 0.0.43, flax 0.12.4, torchax 0.0.13 and tpu-inference, with no PyTorch and no CUDA. tpu-inference is a vLLM plugin, so it still needs a vLLM built for TPU, which the PyPI wheel is not. The supported path is evidently a container or a source build.

text: Taken together, the TPU software ecosystem has sharp edges a GPU user never encounters, and this strengthens the market analysis rather than sitting beside it.
detail: Four independent walls found in one day: SparseCore Pallas unimplemented on v6e while documented as supported, an XLA RET_CHECK on sub-mesh all_reduce, a serving package pinning a nonexistent libtpu, and a CUDA-only vLLM wheel. Third-party TPU serving does not exist for contractual reasons AND because an ordinary user cannot pip install the stack. On a GPU, pip install vllm works.

text: Availability probing works and the first round already shows structure. At 12:12 UTC on a Sunday, a v6e-8 was available in asia-northeast1-b, refused for capacity in five zones, and refused for quota in us-east5-c, which has a zero grant.
detail: Refusal latency ranged from 7 to 218 seconds. The slow refusals are requests that were admitted and rolled back, which is a different failure from an instant rejection, and the distinction is only visible because the probe records elapsed time.

text: Wrote stacks-and-physics.html: the JAX/XLA and PyTorch/CUDA stacks side by side, layer by layer, then the five pieces of arithmetic that predicted every measurement in this study.
detail: Roofline (P <= min(P_peak, I*B), corner at 560 FLOPs/byte on v6e), the transaction-granule correction explaining why the gather is off the roofline entirely, bisection bandwidth (2*min(X,Y) links, which explains the whole scaling curve), Little's law (n >= L/t_op gives n ~ 20, the size of the prize 8i's collectives engine is chasing), and the KV crossover C* = P/(2*L*h_kv*d*b), which is 13k tokens for Qwen3-4B at batch 32 and explains why both vendors split prefill from decode in the same year.

text: The structural difference between the stacks explains why Unsloth has no TPU equivalent. On TPU the compiler owns fusion, layout and collective algorithm selection; on GPU the user owns them via Triton, cuBLAS and NCCL.
detail: Unsloth is a project that beats a default, and the TPU default is already 84.2% of peak on a 4096-cube bf16 matmul, measured here, so a naive port would tie XLA. The primitives for such a port do exist: a blocked Pallas matmul kernel compiles with zero error and a custom VJP for hand-derived backward passes works. The headroom is not dense matmul but MoE routing, activation recomputation and LoRA fusion, which is exactly where Unsloth's own 2026 gains came from.

text: vLLM does run on TPU with an exact version pair: vllm 0.25.0 plus tpu-inference 0.25.0 imports and selects TpuPlatform. A sixth wall then appeared: torchcodec fails to load its shared library and vLLM imports it eagerly even for text-only models.
detail: Six independent ecosystem walls between a student and a served token on TPU: SparseCore unimplemented, XLA RET_CHECK on sub-meshes, tpu-inference 0.26.0 pinning a nonexistent libtpu, a CUDA-only vLLM wheel, the torch/torchax pin conflict, and torchcodec. Each is individually shallow; together they are why third-party TPU serving does not exist, alongside the contractual reason.

text: The A100s are not usable and I should not have counted them. Quota shows 32 on-demand and 64 preemptible in us-west4, but creating an instance fails with 'Required compute.instances.create permission'. We have GPU quota and no GPU permission.
detail: I stated 'we have 32 A100s' several times while planning cross-architecture comparisons. That was read off a quota page and never tested. It is the same mistake this study has now made three times in different clothes, and the pattern is worth naming: quota, capacity and permission are three independent gates, and a number on a quota page is evidence about none of the other two. On this project: v6e spot has all three, v6e on-demand has quota but not permission in us-east1-d, us-east5 has permission but not capacity, and GPUs have quota but not permission anywhere.

text: Stopping the serving thread after five attempts. Wall count reached seven and the last failure was an engine-core init with an empty failed-process set, which is a debugging project rather than a measurement.
detail: Sequence, all real: torchcodec's shared library, then its missing package metadata, then tensor_parallel_size=8 on a host with 4 chips, then a zombie process from my own first import holding the TPU, then an engine core failure. The slice is worth more on the dense-versus-MoE experiment, which needs no serving stack and speaks directly to the study's thesis. The serving attempt is not wasted: the seven walls are the technical half of why third-party TPU serving does not exist.

text: v6e hosts carry 4 chips each, confirmed from vLLM's own device report: a v6e-16 is 4 hosts of 4, a v6e-32 is 8 hosts of 4.
detail: Consequence for serving: single-host tensor parallelism caps at 4 on any v6e slice, and using more chips requires multi-host serving with Ray. Consequence for benchmarking: the JAX process that owns devices in a mesh is not the same as gcloud's worker 0, which is the bug that produced this study's impossible 0.0042 ms measurement.

text: The economics of serving invert with model size, and the two profitable models are exactly the two we cannot run. Break-even throughput needed to match market price: gpt-oss-20b 2,999 tok/s/chip, gpt-oss-120b 2,293, Llama-4-Scout 1,299, DeepSeek-V3.2 975, Llama-4-Maverick 487.
detail: Published v6e throughput for this class is roughly 300 to 1,000 tok/s/chip, so Maverick at 487 and DeepSeek-V3.2 at 975 are inside the achievable range while the small models are hopeless: gpt-oss-20b's price has been competed down to a tenth of a cent per million output tokens. The reason large mixtures pay is that the market charges several times more for them while active parameters stay modest, 17B and 37B. And the cruel part: Maverick needs 32 chips and DeepSeek-V3.2 needs 64, while our working serving path reaches four. The models that fit do not pay; the models that would pay do not fit.

text: I wrote 'every bar clears the band, serving is never economic' into the page before reading the numbers the generator produced. Two of five models fall inside the band.
detail: Caught by rendering the page and looking at it, which is the step that exists precisely for this. The claim was an assumption carried over from the DeepSeek V4 Flash comparison, where break-even was 3,175 tok/s/chip, and I generalised from the cheapest model on the market to all models. Fixed in the published prose.

text: Model selection is now constrained to models listed on OpenRouter, so every candidate has a published price to measure against, and popularity on HuggingFace is explicitly not a criterion.
detail: HuggingFace trending is dominated by models we cannot run: the current flagship is Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B at 2.4 trillion parameters, needing about ninety v6e chips. Most-downloaded is the opposite extreme, dominated by sub-8B models. Neither list tells us what is worth measuring. A published price does.

text: Cannot request IAM roles programmatically: there is no request API, Privileged Access Manager is not configured on this project, and self-granting returns 'does not have permission'.
detail: The grantors are identifiable from the project labels: su__smjones is owner, technical contact and requester of record; su__tbrooke is the financial contact. Drafted the request in OUTREACH.md with the exact two gcloud commands so it is a thirty-second job for them, and ranked the asks: billing.viewer is read-only, cannot affect anyone's workloads, and answers a question nobody on the project can currently answer, which is how much credit is left. container.admin is the larger grant and is offered as optional, with manifests handed over either way.

text: A TPU gather runs 3.3x slower above a buffer-size threshold, and the threshold is a compiler decision, not a memory-system effect
detail: v5p steps 256->77 GB/s between a 40 and 48 MiB buffer; v6e steps 154->42 GB/s between 80 and 96 MiB. Holding allocation fixed and widening the touched span 2->128 MiB changes nothing (76.5-76.8 GB/s). Sorting or block-grouping the indices changes nothing. Only the declared buffer size matters. The optimised HLO shows why: below the threshold the gather operand carries the S(1) memory-space annotation and above it does not, so XLA promotes the table on chip at compile time from the declared shape alone, before any index exists.

text: The promotion threshold is exactly 50,266,112 bytes on v5p and 100,597,760 on v6e, both 64 KiB under a round power-of-two, and it can be found with zero kernel time
detail: Identical across 128-, 256- and 512-wide rows, so it is a byte budget rather than a row count; at 64-wide rows it halves because f32 lays out in T(8,128) tiles and a 64-wide row wastes half of every tile, so the budget counts padded bytes. Bisected by compiling and grepping for S(1), no benchmark and no allocation needed. v5p has 2 TensorCores per chip and v6e has 1, and 48x2 = 96, which is a hypothesis rather than a result.

text: My arithmetic that the budget covered table plus indices was wrong, and only looked right because 4n happened to equal 64 KiB at the one shape I checked
detail: Growing the index vector 64x, from n=1024 to n=65536, left the table threshold at 50,266,112 bytes on v5p and 100,597,760 on v6e, unchanged in every case. So the 64 KiB is a fixed reservation of unknown origin. Tested because the coincidence looked too tidy, which is the only reason it got caught.

text: An A100 shows the mirror image: flat in declared buffer size, mildly sensitive to real footprint
detail: 222-236 GB/s across a 24x range of buffer size, a 1.06x spread, against the TPU's 3.3x step. Allocation control: 221 GB/s in a 32 MiB buffer vs 215 in a 128 MiB buffer at the same 32 MiB span, i.e. nothing. Span 2->128 MiB at fixed allocation: 245->215 GB/s, a 1.14x fall, which is L2 doing real work. So the TPU is blind to the two runtime facts and sensitive to the compile-time artefact, and the GPU is the exact inverse. Only one of those two failure modes is fixable in a compiler.

text: GKE Autopilot provisions GPUs on a project where our own identity is denied compute.instances.create
detail: A pod requesting nvidia-tesla-a100 triggered TriggeredScaleUp and an a2-highgpu-1g node appeared in us-west4-b. The node is created by the GKE service agent, not by us, so the IAM denial that blocked direct VM creation does not apply. Fourth distinct gate found: quota, capacity, permission, and now which service account does the creating. Practical consequence for a student on a shared class project: ask Kubernetes, not Compute Engine.

text: Modal is unusable for the H100 comparison: workspace spend limit exceeded
detail: Valid credentials, authenticated profile, a deployed app, and no credit. The class GCP project has A100 16-32 and L4 32 quota in eight regions but zero H100 quota anywhere, so an H100 number needs either a raised Modal limit or Stanford Marlowe, which is 248 H100s behind a PI-sponsored allocation.

text: The contention log and cluster dashboard were misreporting who holds the cluster, and the budget guard was inventing spend
detail: observe_contention.py identified our slices by a hardcoded set of VM names from a fleet deleted hours earlier, so every slice we own except anh-dev1 counted as a peer's: it logged '32 chips held by 3 peers' when the truth was 8 held by 1. Separately, all three scripts read the number in an accelerator type as a chip count, but v5p and v4 count TensorCores and put two per chip, so v5p-8 is four chips and not eight. The budget guard compounded that by having no v5p rate and falling back to v6e's, billing our v5p at 11.23/hr against a real 5.04, about 2,400 dollars of imaginary spend before September and enough to trigger a false STOP. Ownership is now by prefix and chip counts go through one documented helper. Corrected runway: 582 hr at the steady fleet against 375 hr needed to reach Sep 1.

text: The campaign had been dead for four hours and the schedule could not recover on its own
detail: A cycle wedged at 12:53Z on a --worker=all ssh and held the lock. launchd does not start a second copy of a job while the first is alive, so every scheduled cycle after it exited immediately and the site stopped updating. Fixed with a deadline on all 24 network calls, remote-side timeouts, a 1500s whole-cycle watchdog, an orphaned-gcloud reaper, and pushing whenever local is ahead of origin rather than only when files changed. The first version of the timeout helper had two bugs of its own, found by testing it: the killer subshell inherited the command-substitution pipe so every wrapped call blocked for its full deadline after succeeding, and long-lived killers could fire kill -9 at a recycled pid.

text: The publish step was being starved by the availability probe, which is why two finished pages sat unpublished
detail: probe_availability.sh ended with a bare wait on backgrounded TPU deletes. A probe slice in asia-northeast1-b took over twelve minutes to delete, the wait blocked on it, the probe consumed nearly the whole 1500s cycle budget, and the watchdog killed the cycle before it could publish. Fixed three ways: the probe no longer waits and instead reaps leftovers at the start of each run, which also catches slices left by a killed cycle; every publish stage now has its own deadline; and publishing runs in two passes, local pages pushed first and the live scrape after, so anything generated without the network ships before anything that needs it.

text: Steady fleet moved from 16 v6e chips to 16 v5p chips, which is cheaper and better matched to the study
detail: v5p is the only generation where the SparseCore gather kernel compiles, its 3D torus tests the bisection-bandwidth model on a second topology, and on spot it is 1.26 per chip-hour against v6e's 1.4033. So 16 v5p chips cost 20.16/hr against the 22.45/hr of the 16 v6e chips they replace: the Sept 1 runway improved from 582 to 632 hours while the hardware got more relevant. anh-dev1, a single v6e chip, stays because the gather-cliff comparison needs a second generation and that measurement is single-chip anyway. There is no v6p; the sixth generation shipped only v6e, so v5p's 95 GB per chip is the largest-memory chip obtainable until Ironwood.

text: The orphaned-gcloud reaper never worked: macOS ps has no etimes keyword
detail: It used ps -o etimes=, which on macOS makes ps print its whole keyword list to stderr and return nothing, so the age test always failed the numeric guard and reaped nothing while filling launchd.err.log with 'integer expression expected'. macOS only has etime, formatted [[DD-]HH:]MM:SS. Now parsed with awk and unit-tested: 0s for self, 62326s for launchd, empty for a nonexistent pid. Worth noting that this was one of four protections added specifically to keep the campaign alive, and it was the one that was silently broken.

text: Publishing is blocked: git has no stored GitHub credential, and the site now says so on its own front page
detail: git push fails with 'could not read Username for https://github.com: Device not configured', which means the credential helper returned nothing and there was no terminal to prompt on. It fails identically from a launchd cycle and from an interactive shell with the sandbox disabled, so it is the credential and not the environment. A push succeeded at 15:53 UTC (commit ab09e0f) so the entry existed earlier today. Measurements are unaffected and accumulate locally; the ahead-of-origin check means one successful push ships all of them. Because a page that regenerates every twenty minutes but cannot publish looks live while being stale, index.html now carries a banner stating how many commits are unpushed and when the visible version was published. Fix needs a human: gh auth login, then gh auth setup-git.

text: Bisection bandwidth does not explain all_to_all cost on a 3D torus, and one configuration rules it out outright
detail: On the v5p-32, dims [2,2,4], eight chips were selected four ways so that count, payload, code and compiler were identical and only geometry differed. Computed from the coordinates, the set z in {0,2} has a bisection of ZERO links: its two 2x2 planes are not adjacent, so it owns no link between its halves. It ran at 0.1889 ms, statistically identical to the contiguous 2x2x2 cube at 0.1878 ms, while the two slabs with bisection 4 ran 44 percent slower. Holding bisection at 2 and chip count at 4, spanning one host took 0.1872 ms, two hosts 0.1798 ms, and four hosts 0.2565 ms. Across all eight configurations the split is at most two hosts fast, 0.180 to 0.189 ms, versus four hosts slow, 0.256 to 0.278 ms, independent of chip count being 4, 8 or 16 and independent of bisection being 0, 2, 4 or 8. Caveat stated rather than hidden: on this slice each host owns exactly one z-plane, so host span, span along the length-4 axis, and the fraction of the mesh the timing process owns are perfectly confounded and this experiment cannot separate them. What it does settle is that chip-adjacency bisection is not the mechanism, and that the earlier 8-to-16-chip comparisons silently changed host count at the same time as chip count.
